past_medical_history: IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) — diagnosed 2 years ago by hematology
family_history: No family history of neuropathy or blood disorders

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive bilateral distal leg and foot numbness with gait instability over 3 years — hematologist referred to neurology given IgM MGUS
patient.history_present_illness: A 68-year-old retired banker with IgM MGUS (IgM paraprotein 0.8 g/dL, diagnosed 2 years ago by hematology during a routine evaluation for mildly elevated total protein) presented to neurology clinic for evaluation of progressive bilateral foot and leg numbness and gait instability. He notes the onset of numbness was gradual over approximately three years — he initially noticed tingling and reduced sensation in both feet, which progressively worsened and is now at mid-calf level. He has become increasingly unsteady on his feet, particularly in the dark or on uneven surfaces, and has had two near-falls. He does not describe significant pain — the predominant symptom is numbness and profound unsteadiness. He has also noticed increasing difficulty with fine finger tasks — he struggles with small buttons and has difficulty feeling the keys on his keyboard. His wife notes that he has a distinctive wobbly gait with exaggerated arm movements for balance. His IgM MGUS was being followed with annual monitoring; hematology detected a slightly larger paraprotein (0.8 → 1.1 g/dL) on the most recent value 3 months ago and referred him to neurology given concern for paraprotein-associated neuropathy. He denies constitutional symptoms — no fever, night sweats, or unintentional weight loss.

neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral distal weakness — toe extension 4/5 bilaterally, ankle dorsiflexion 4+/5. Mild bilateral hand intrinsic weakness (grip 4+/5). Proximal strength normal.
neurological_exam.sensory: Severe proprioceptive loss bilateral great toes and ankles — cannot detect 1 cm movement. Vibration absent at great toes and ankles bilaterally. Reduced vibration at mid-calf. Light touch and pinprick — stocking pattern to knees, glove to wrists. Touch grossly preserved but proprioception disproportionately impaired.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Ankle reflexes absent. Knee jerks absent. Biceps and brachioradialis 1+. Triceps trace. Plantar flexors bilaterally.
neurological_exam.coordination: Heel-shin — marked sensory ataxia, unable to complete. Finger-nose: mild inaccuracy due to proprioceptive loss.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based sensory ataxia. Romberg markedly positive (falls within seconds of eye closure). Steppage component. Cannot tandem walk. Uses arms widely for balance.
neurological_exam.additional: No pes cavus. No organomegaly appreciated on brief inspection. No peripheral adenopathy.

Neuropathy_workup.value: IgM paraprotein 1.1 g/dL (increased from 0.8 g/dL 6 months ago)

quantitative_data.pattern: Predominantly demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy — markedly prolonged distal motor latencies and slow velocities, especially distally; characteristic 'terminal slowing' of anti-MAG neuropathy

specialized_test.impression: Demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy with markedly prolonged distal motor latencies (DML) — characteristic pattern of anti-MAG neuropathy. The disproportionate prolongation of distal motor latency (DML 8.6-9.2 ms, well above normal <5 ms) with relatively preserved proximal conduction is the hallmark of anti-MAG/IgM paraprotein neuropathy. Minimal acute denervation on EMG — predominantly demyelinating. This NCS pattern combined with anti-MAG antibody titer 1:102,400 is diagnostic.
recommended_actions: Anti-MAG neuropathy confirmed — hematology referral for IgM MGUS management and potential rituximab therapy
Neuroprotection: avoid falls, physical therapy for balance

results.title: Anti-MAG neuropathy — rituximab treatment and outcomes
results.key_finding: Rituximab reduces anti-MAG antibody titers and stabilizes anti-MAG neuropathy in 40-50% of patients; improvement is partial and slow (6-12 months); early treatment associated with better outcomes

results.title: IgM MGUS progression to Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia
results.key_finding: IgM paraprotein >1.5 g/dL or increasing trend warrants bone marrow biopsy to exclude Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia; IgM 1.1 g/dL with increasing trend requires monitoring

output.summary: Anti-MAG neuropathy is treated with B-cell depleting therapy (rituximab) in symptomatic patients. The IgM paraprotein 1.1 g/dL (increasing from 0.8) warrants bone marrow biopsy to exclude Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia. Rituximab 375 mg/m2 x4 cycles is standard. Partial stabilization/improvement expected in 40-50% of patients.

output.test_type: Bone marrow biopsy with flow cytometry (hematology-performed)

findings.finding: Bone marrow cellularity 30% (normal for age). CD20+ B-cell clone detected — small lymphoplasmacytic population <5% of marrow cellularity. No evidence of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (requires >10% lymphoplasmacytic infiltration).
Flow cytometry: IgM kappa expressing B-cell clone confirmed; no high-grade lymphoma

output.impression: IgM MGUS confirmed — not Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia (lymphoplasmacytic infiltration <5%). However, the increasing IgM paraprotein and anti-MAG neuropathy indication for rituximab treatment is present regardless of this result. Hematology will discuss rituximab candidacy.
recommended_actions: Rituximab therapy discussion with hematology for anti-MAG neuropathy

results.title: Anti-MAG neuropathy — long-term natural history
results.key_finding: Anti-MAG neuropathy is typically slowly progressive; majority remain ambulatory at 10 years but with significant disability; rituximab can stabilize or partially improve in 40-50%

output.summary: Anti-MAG neuropathy tends to be slowly progressive. Most patients remain ambulatory but disability accumulates over years. Early treatment with rituximab is recommended for progressive disability. This patient's severe proprioceptive loss and high fall risk indicate significant current disability warranting treatment.

differential.key_features: Anti-MAG neuropathy NCS pattern shows disproportionate distal slowing (terminal slowing) rather than uniform CIDP demyelination; CIDP is proximal and distal; anti-MAG is predominantly terminal; anti-MAG antibody positive 1:102,400 is diagnostic
No family history; adult onset; IgM paraprotein positive; anti-MAG positive — acquired neuropathy
HbA1c 5.6% — no diabetes. IgM anti-MAG is the primary etiology.
Bone marrow biopsy shows <5% lymphoplasmacytic infiltration — IgM MGUS, not WM

critical_actions: Anti-MAG antibody testing is essential in any IgM MGUS patient with neuropathy

contraindicated_actions: IVIG as primary treatment for anti-MAG neuropathy — less effective than rituximab; rituximab is first-line
Prednisone/oral steroids alone — anti-MAG neuropathy does not respond well to steroids
Treating as CIDP without checking anti-MAG antibodies in IgM MGUS patient
key_reasoning_points: Anti-MAG neuropathy is diagnosed by: (1) IgM kappa MGUS, (2) anti-MAG antibody titer >1:10,000, (3) characteristic NCS with disproportionately prolonged distal motor latencies
The NCS pattern of 'terminal slowing' (DML markedly prolonged vs preserved proximal conduction) distinguishes anti-MAG from CIDP
Proprioceptive loss with sensory ataxia is the dominant clinical feature — different from painful diabetic neuropathy
Rituximab is the primary disease-modifying treatment — reduces anti-MAG titers in 40-50% of patients

red_herrings.intended_effect: IVIG treatment initiated for presumed CIDP without checking anti-MAG antibodies
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The NCS pattern — disproportionately prolonged DML with relatively preserved proximal velocity — is the 'terminal slowing' hallmark of anti-MAG neuropathy. In any demyelinating neuropathy with IgM paraprotein, anti-MAG must be tested.
